identity.title: HINTS (head impulse, nystagmus, test of skew) — ACUTE VESTIBULAR SYNDROME ONLY; validated by neuro-ophthalmologists

technique.how: Only in acute vestibular syndrome (continuous vertigo, spontaneous nystagmus, gait unsteadiness). Three steps: (1) horizontal head impulse test looking for a corrective saccade; (2) nystagmus in primary and 30-degree lateral gaze looking for direction change; (3) alternate cover test looking for vertical refixation (skew). Benign = abnormal HIT + unidirectional nystagmus + no skew.
technique.prerequisites: Spontaneous nystagmus present; alert, cooperative patient who can fixate; examiner trained in eliciting and reading corrective saccades and skew.
technique.contraindications: Cervical spine instability or dissection concern for the impulse component; not applicable when nystagmus is absent (episodic, positional, or resolved vertigo).

interpretation.positive_finding: Dangerous HINTS = any of normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation: 100% sensitive and 96% specific for a central lesion in the original expert cohort (LR+ 25), pooled 96.7%/94.8% when performed by neurologists.
interpretation.negative_finding: Benign HINTS (abnormal HIT, unidirectional nystagmus, no skew) in expert hands nearly excludes stroke (LR- about 0.00-0.04); in mixed emergency-physician cohorts sensitivity fell to 83% with specificity 44%, so a benign result by a non-expert does not rule out stroke.
interpretation.pitfalls: Applying HINTS to patients without nystagmus, to episodic or positional vertigo, or with untrained examiners yields misleading results; AICA strokes can give an abnormal HIT. Truncal ataxia without nystagmus is a central presentation HINTS does not capture, so always add gait assessment.
interpretation.changes_what: Dangerous HINTS in AVS: stroke pathway and MRI. Benign HINTS by an expert with normal gait: vestibular neuritis, imaging can be deferred; by a non-expert it should not replace MRI.

estimates.target_condition: Central lesion (ischemic stroke, hemorrhage, other) in acute vestibular syndrome; dangerous HINTS
estimates.population: 101 consecutive AVS patients with >=1 stroke risk factor (25 peripheral, 76 central); examiners = neurologist/neuro-ophthalmologist (original derivation cohort)
estimates.reference_standard: MRI (DWI) or CT plus clinical follow-up; peripheral lesions required normal MRI
estimates.quote: dangerous H.I.N.T.S. result was 100% sensitive and 96% specific for the presence of a central lesion, giving a positive likelihood ratio of 25 (95%CI 3.66-170.59)
estimates.location: Results text, PMC4593511 (same sentence continues 'negative likelihood ratio of 0.00 (95%CI 0.00-0.11)'); Table 4 row 'Dangerous bedside H.I.N.T.S. 100% 96% 0.00 (0.00-0.12)'

estimates.target_condition: Central cause of vertigo (vertebrobasilar stroke, ICH) in ED patients with acute vestibular syndrome; HINTS performed by NEUROLOGISTS
estimates.population: Pooled prospective ED AVS studies (5 studies, 617 participants overall); neurologist-examined subset
estimates.computed_from: LRs computed from pooled sens 0.967 and spec 0.948: LR+ = 0.967/0.052 = 18.6; LR- = 0.033/0.948 = 0.035. Prevalence = reported mean stroke prevalence 39.1% across included studies.
estimates.quote: performed by neurologists, had a sensitivity of 96.7% (95% CI = 93.1% to 98.5% ...) and specificity of 94.8% (95% CI = 91% to 97.1%)

estimates.target_condition: Central cause of vertigo in ED patients with acute vestibular syndrome; HINTS performed by a MIXED cohort of board-certified EMERGENCY PHYSICIANS and neurologists
estimates.population: Pooled prospective ED AVS studies in which examiners included emergency physicians (non-neuro-otologist) as well as neurologists
estimates.computed_from: LRs computed from sens 0.83 and spec 0.44: LR+ = 0.83/0.56 = 1.48; LR- = 0.17/0.44 = 0.39.
estimates.quote: the sensitivity was 83% (95% CI = 63% to 95%) and specificity was 44% (95% CI = 36% to 51%)
estimates.location: Abstract, Results (cohort including both emergency physicians and neurologists)

estimates.target_condition: Posterior-circulation stroke (any stroke) in acute vestibular syndrome; positive HINTS
estimates.population: 6 studies, 644 AVS patients, 200 with MRI-confirmed stroke; examiner expertise mixed across studies (mostly neurology/neuro-otology)
estimates.computed_from: LRs computed from pooled sens 0.955 and spec 0.712: LR+ = 0.955/0.288 = 3.32; LR- = 0.045/0.712 = 0.063. Prevalence = 200/644.
estimates.quote: For any stroke, the pooled sensitivity was 95.5% (95% CI: 92.6-98.4%) and specificity was 71.2% (95% CI: 67.0-75.4%)

sources.citation: Kattah JC, Talkad AV, Wang DZ, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. HINTS to diagnose stroke in the acute vestibular syndrome: three-step bedside oculomotor examination more sensitive than early MRI diffusion-weighted imaging. Stroke. 2009;40(11):3504-3510.

Ohle R, Montpellier RA, Marchadier V, Wharton A, McIsaac S, Anderson M, Savage D. Can Emergency Physicians Accurately Rule Out a Central Cause of Vertigo Using the HINTS Examination? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Acad Emerg Med. 2020;27(9):887-896.

Krishnan K, Bassilious K, Eriksen E, et al. Posterior circulation stroke diagnosis using HINTS in patients presenting with acute vestibular syndrome: A systematic review. Eur Stroke J. 2019;4(3):233-239.

Tarnutzer AA, Berkowitz AL, Robinson KA, Hsieh YH, Newman-Toker DE. Does my dizzy patient have a stroke? A systematic review of bedside diagnosis in acute vestibular syndrome. CMAJ. 2011;183(9):E571-E592.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Never apply outside acute vestibular syndrome (no spontaneous nystagmus, episodic/positional/resolved vertigo) and never let a benign HINTS by an untrained examiner replace imaging in a patient with stroke risk factors or gait failure.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Any dangerous component (normal HIT, direction-changing nystagmus, skew) or inability to stand is a posterior-circulation stroke until MRI proves otherwise; early DWI is falsely negative in about 12%.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Accuracy is examiner-dependent: neurologist/neuro-otologist pooled sens 0.967/spec 0.948 vs mixed emergency-physician cohort sens 0.83/spec 0.44 (Ohle 2020); the two must not be averaged or applied interchangeably.

extraction_notes: Scope: HINTS applies ONLY to acute vestibular syndrome. Estimates deliberately split by examiner expertise (Kattah 2009 derivation cohort with expert examiners; Ohle 2020 neurologist-only pooled vs mixed emergency-physician cohort) and never averaged. Ohle's ED-physician figure comes from a cohort that combined board-certified emergency physicians with neurologists, so it is labelled as such rather than as pure EP performance. Ohle journal year is 2020 (epub) with PubMed listing 2021 volume; Krishnan epub 2019 (PubMed 2022 listing). Kattah LR- (0.00, CI 0.00-0.11) is in the same Results sentence as the quoted LR+ but omitted from the quote for the 25-word limit; Table 4 gives CI upper 0.12. Ohle quote uses an ellipsis to drop 'I2 = 0%' for length. All LRs from the meta-analyses are computed from pooled sens/spec.
